claim: Non-overlapping cell populations within dorsomedial prefrontal cortex (dmPFC), defined by gene expression or projection target, control dissociable aspects of reward seeking through unique activity patterns.
source: Non-overlapping cell populations within dorsomedial prefrontal cortex (dmPFC), defined by gene expression or projection target, control dissociable aspects of reward seeking through unique activity patterns.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to established findings in the field, as indicated by the context of prior research.

claim: Even within defined cell populations in dmPFC, considerable cell-to-cell variability is found.
source: However, even within these defined cell populations, considerable cell-to-cell variability is found, suggesting that greater resolution is needed to understand information processing in dmPFC.
evidence: This is stated as an observation that motivates the current study.

claim: Five unique neuronal ensembles exist in dmPFC that each encode specialized information related to a sucrose reward, reward-predictive cues, and behavioral responses to those cues.
source: We characterize five unique neuronal ensembles that each encodes specialized information related to a sucrose reward, reward-predictive cues, and behavioral responses to those cues.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from two-photon calcium imaging and clustering analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The neuronal ensembles differentially emerge across daily training sessions and stabilize after learning.
source: The ensembles differentially emerge across daily training sessions – and stabilize after learning – in a manner that improves the predictive validity of dmPFC activity dynamics for deciphering variables related to behavioral conditioning.
evidence: This is supported by longitudinal tracking data showing changes in ensemble activity from early to late learning sessions.

claim: The emergence and stabilization of ensembles improves the predictive validity of dmPFC activity dynamics for deciphering variables related to behavioral conditioning.
source: The ensembles differentially emerge across daily training sessions – and stabilize after learning – in a manner that improves the predictive validity of dmPFC activity dynamics for deciphering variables related to behavioral conditioning.
evidence: This is supported by decoding analyses showing improved prediction of behavioral variables after learning.

claim: dmPFC neuronal ensemble dynamics stably predict reward availability and initiation of conditioned reward seeking following cue-reward learning.
source: Our results characterize the complex dmPFC neuronal ensemble dynamics that stably predict reward availability and initiation of conditioned reward seeking following cue-reward learning.
evidence: This is supported by decoding analyses and stability measurements across sessions after learning.

claim: The dorsomedial prefrontal cortex (dmPFC) is dysregulated in diseases associated with disordered reward processing.
source: The dorsomedial prefrontal cortex (dmPFC) has garnered considerable interest due to its dysregulation in diseases associated with disordered reward processing (Chen et al., 2018; Courchesne et al., 2011; Dienel and Lewis, 2019; Holmes et al., 2018; Koob and Volkow, 2010; Ye et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: dmPFC abnormalities include aberrant cell morphology and regional mass.
source: These abnormalities include aberrant cell morphology and regional mass (Courchesne et al., 2011), abnormal activity patterns (Dienel and Lewis, 2019), and reduced behavioral performance on tasks that involve dmPFC activity (Goldstein and Volkow, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Courchesne et al., 2011.

claim: dmPFC abnormalities include abnormal activity patterns.
source: These abnormalities include aberrant cell morphology and regional mass (Courchesne et al., 2011), abnormal activity patterns (Dienel and Lewis, 2019), and reduced behavioral performance on tasks that involve dmPFC activity (Goldstein and Volkow, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dienel and Lewis, 2019.

claim: dmPFC abnormalities include reduced behavioral performance on tasks that involve dmPFC activity.
source: These abnormalities include aberrant cell morphology and regional mass (Courchesne et al., 2011), abnormal activity patterns (Dienel and Lewis, 2019), and reduced behavioral performance on tasks that involve dmPFC activity (Goldstein and Volkow, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Goldstein and Volkow, 2011.

claim: Neuronal activity in dmPFC neurons is observed to be heterogeneous in a variety of behavioral tasks.
source: Neuronal activity in dmPFC neurons is observed to be heterogeneous in a variety of behavioral tasks (Kim et al., 2016; Kobayashi et al., 2006; Matsumoto et al., 2003; Powell and Redish, 2014), including those that involve reward-seeking behaviors (Sun et al., 2011; Moorman and Aston-Jones, 2015; Otis et al., 2017; Otis et al., 2019; Sparta et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Recent studies have aimed to resolve dmPFC heterogeneity through cell-type specific recording strategies, such as in vivo calcium imaging in genetically or projection-defined neurons.
source: Recent studies have aimed to resolve this heterogeneity through cell-type specific recording strategies, such as in vivo calcium imaging in genetically or projection-defined neurons (Otis et al., 2017; Otis et al., 2019; Siciliano et al., 2019; Ye et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: A vast majority of response diversity in dmPFC remains unexplained even when accounting for identified neuronal subpopulations.
source: Although some variability can be explained by identified neuronal subpopulations, a vast majority of response diversity remains unexplained (Otis et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Otis et al., 2017.

claim: About two-thirds of dmPFC excitatory neurons that project to the nucleus accumbens (NAc) show excitatory responses to reward-predictive cues, while about one-third show inhibitory responses.
source: For example, we recently demonstrated that many dmPFC excitatory neurons that project to the nucleus accumbens (NAc) show diverse responses to reward-predictive cues, with about two-thirds of the responding cells being excitatory responders and the other third being inhibitory responders.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from prior work by the authors.

claim: About two-thirds of dmPFC neurons that project to the paraventricular thalamus (PVT) show inhibitory responses to reward-predictive cues, while about one-third show excitatory responses.
source: Similarly, dmPFC neurons that project to the paraventricular thalamus (PVT) also show diverse responses to reward-predictive cues, with about two-thirds of responding cells being inhibitory responders and the other one-third being excitatory responders (Otis et al., 2017; Otis et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Otis et al., 2017 and 2019.

claim: Mice readily acquired the Pavlovian conditioned licking task across sessions.
source: Mice readily acquired this task across sessions (one session per day; see Figure 1—figure supplement 1), showing conditioned licking behavior between the CS+ offset and reward delivery (trace interval), but not the CS- offset and equivalent no-reward epoch during sessions on later days (deemed 'late in learning'; Figure 1C–D).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mice showed conditioned licking behavior between the CS+ offset and reward delivery (trace interval) during late learning sessions.
source: Mice readily acquired this task across sessions (one session per day; see Figure 1—figure supplement 1), showing conditioned licking behavior between the CS+ offset and reward delivery (trace interval), but not the CS- offset and equivalent no-reward epoch during sessions on later days (deemed 'late in learning'; Figure 1C–D).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1C-D.

claim: Mice did not show conditioned licking behavior during the CS- offset and equivalent no-reward epoch during late learning sessions.
source: Mice readily acquired this task across sessions (one session per day; see Figure 1—figure supplement 1), showing conditioned licking behavior between the CS+ offset and reward delivery (trace interval), but not the CS- offset and equivalent no-reward epoch during sessions on later days (deemed 'late in learning'; Figure 1C–D).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1C-D.

claim: A two-way ANOVA revealed a significant cue by session interaction for conditioned licking behavior (F1,47 = 165.1; p-value < 0.001).
source: A two-way ANOVA revealed a significant cue by session interaction for conditioned licking behavior (Δ lick rate; F1,47 = 165.1; p-value < 0.001), and post hoc tests confirmed that mice licked significantly more during CS+ trials during late in learning sessions as compared with CS- trials during both sessions (p-values < 0.001) and CS+ trials during early in learning sessions (p-value < 0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the behavioral data analysis.

claim: Mice licked significantly more during CS+ trials during late in learning sessions as compared with CS- trials during both sessions (p-values < 0.001).
source: A two-way ANOVA revealed a significant cue by session interaction for conditioned licking behavior (Δ lick rate; F1,47 = 165.1; p-value < 0.001), and post hoc tests confirmed that mice licked significantly more during CS+ trials during late in learning sessions as compared with CS- trials during both sessions (p-values < 0.001) and CS+ trials during early in learning sessions (p-value < 0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical result from post hoc tests.

claim: Mice licked significantly more during CS+ trials during late in learning sessions as compared with CS+ trials during early in learning sessions (p-value < 0.001).
source: A two-way ANOVA revealed a significant cue by session interaction for conditioned licking behavior (Δ lick rate; F1,47 = 165.1; p-value < 0.001), and post hoc tests confirmed that mice licked significantly more during CS+ trials during late in learning sessions as compared with CS- trials during both sessions (p-values < 0.001) and CS+ trials during early in learning sessions (p-value < 0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical result from post hoc tests.

claim: Conditioned licking behavior for the CS+, but not CS-, developed across days of training, revealing that the cue-reward association had been acquired by sessions identified as 'late in learning'.
source: Thus, conditioned licking behavior for the CS+, but not CS-, developed across days of training revealing that the cue-reward association had been acquired by sessions identified as 'late in learning'.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the behavioral data showing differential licking responses to CS+ vs CS-.

claim: Cluster 1 neurons show excitatory responses during CS+, CS-, and reward delivery (n = 192 neurons from 5/7 mice; 17/21 FOVs).
source: Cluster 1: excitatory responses during CS+, CS-, and reward delivery (n = 192 neurons from 5/7 mice; 17/21 FOVs)
evidence: This is based on qualitative analysis of activity patterns shown in Figure 1H and J.

claim: Cluster 2 neurons show excitatory responses during CS+ trials (n = 346 neurons from 7/7 mice; 19/21 FOVs).
source: Cluster 2: excitatory responses during CS+ trials (n = 346 neurons from 7/7 mice; 19/21 FOVs)
evidence: This is based on qualitative analysis of activity patterns shown in Figure 1H and J.

claim: Cluster 3 neurons show excitatory responses during CS+ and CS- trials (n = 291 neurons from 7/7 mice; 20/21 FOVs).
source: Cluster 3: excitatory responses during CS+ and CS- trials (n = 291 neurons from 7/7 mice; 20/21 FOVs)
evidence: This is based on qualitative analysis of activity patterns shown in Figure 1H and J.

claim: Cluster 4 neurons show excitatory responses during reward delivery (n = 320 neurons from 5/7 mice; 17/21 FOVs).
source: Cluster 4: excitatory responses during reward delivery (n = 320 neurons from 5/7 mice; 17/21 FOVs)
evidence: This is based on qualitative analysis of activity patterns shown in Figure 1H and J.

claim: Cluster 5 neurons show inhibitory responses during CS+ trials (n = 362 neurons; 7/7 mice; 21/21 FOVs).
source: Cluster 5: inhibitory responses during CS+ trials (n = 362 neurons; 7/7 mice; 21/21 FOVs)
evidence: This is based on qualitative analysis of activity patterns shown in Figure 1H and J.

claim: The proportion of neurons within Cluster 5 positively predicts cue discrimination licking scores (p-value = 0.012).
source: Pearson-R correlation values, found in the inset of each subpanel (Figure 2A), reveal a significant, positive relationship between cue discrimination licking scores and the percentage of neurons in Cluster 5 (p-value = 0.012).
evidence: This is a statistical result from correlation analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: There was no significant correlation between cue discrimination licking scores and the percentage of neurons in Clusters 1–4 (p-values > 0.2).
source: However, there was no significant correlation found for Clusters 1–4 (p-values > 0.2).
evidence: This is a statistical result from correlation analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Mice with greater numbers of neurons displaying inhibitory CS+ responses after learning, as in Cluster 5, may have improved behavioral performance in the appetitive learning task.
source: These findings suggest that mice with greater numbers of neurons displaying inhibitory CS+ responses after learning, as in Cluster 5, may have improved behavioral performance in the appetitive learning task.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the correlation between Cluster 5 proportion and behavioral performance.

claim: The relative proportion of neurons within Cluster 3 positively predicts an increase in licking during CS- trials (p-value = 0.009).
source: Pearson-R correlation values, found in each subpanel (Figure 2B), reveal a significant, positive relationship between the initiation of CS- licking 'errors' and the percentage of neurons in Cluster 3 (p-value = 0.009).
evidence: This is a statistical result from correlation analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: There was no significant correlation between CS- licking errors and the percentage of neurons in other clusters (p-values > 0.2).
source: However, there was no significant correlation found for other clusters (p-values > 0.2).
evidence: This is a statistical result from correlation analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Mice with greater numbers of neurons that display equivalent, excitatory responses to both cues, as in Cluster 3, may be more likely to initiate reward seeking when rewards are not available.
source: These data suggest that mice with greater numbers of neurons that display equivalent, excitatory responses to both cues, as in Cluster 3, may be more likely to initiate reward seeking when rewards are not available.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the correlation between Cluster 3 proportion and CS- licking errors.

claim: dmPFC population dynamics within each FOV can be used to detect the presentation of the CS+, CS-, CS+ vs. CS- (cue discrimination), reward, and licking rate during late in learning sessions.
source: Overall, we find that dmPFC population dynamics within each FOV can be used to detect the presentation of the CS+, CS-, CS+ vs. CS- (cue discrimination), reward, and licking rate during late in learning sessions, whereas these activity patterns can be used to predict only the CS+, CS-, and CS+ vs. CS- (cue discrimination), but not reward delivery or licking rate during early in learning sessions (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by decoding analysis results shown in Figure 3A.

claim: dmPFC activity patterns can be used to predict only the CS+, CS-, and CS+ vs. CS- (cue discrimination), but not reward delivery or licking rate during early in learning sessions.
source: Overall, we find that dmPFC population dynamics within each FOV can be used to detect the presentation of the CS+, CS-, CS+ vs. CS- (cue discrimination), reward, and licking rate during late in learning sessions, whereas these activity patterns can be used to predict only the CS+, CS-, and CS+ vs. CS- (cue discrimination), but not reward delivery or licking rate during early in learning sessions (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by decoding analysis results shown in Figure 3A.

claim: There was improved CS+ detection across learning (post hoc p-value = 0.020).
source: A heat map illustrating normalized decoding early and late in learning, and the change in that decoding across learning, reveals improved CS+ detection (post hoc p-value = 0.020), reward detection (post hoc p-value = 0.020), and lick rate prediction across learning (post hoc p-value = 0.009; other p-values > 0.37; Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a statistical result from decoding analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: There was improved reward detection across learning (post hoc p-value = 0.020).
source: A heat map illustrating normalized decoding early and late in learning, and the change in that decoding across learning, reveals improved CS+ detection (post hoc p-value = 0.020), reward detection (post hoc p-value = 0.020), and lick rate prediction across learning (post hoc p-value = 0.009; other p-values > 0.37; Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a statistical result from decoding analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: There was improved lick rate prediction across learning (post hoc p-value = 0.009).
source: A heat map illustrating normalized decoding early and late in learning, and the change in that decoding across learning, reveals improved CS+ detection (post hoc p-value = 0.020), reward detection (post hoc p-value = 0.020), and lick rate prediction across learning (post hoc p-value = 0.009; other p-values > 0.37; Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a statistical result from decoding analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The activity dynamics of dmPFC excitatory output neurons can be used for cue detection, cue discrimination, reward detection, and prediction of licking after learning.
source: Overall, the activity dynamics of dmPFC excitatory output neurons can be used for cue detection, cue discrimination, reward detection, and prediction of licking after learning.
evidence: This is a summary of the decoding analysis results.

claim: Activity in dmPFC excitatory output neurons cannot be used to accurately infer reward delivery or licking during sessions early in learning.
source: However, activity in these neurons cannot be used to accurately infer reward delivery or licking during sessions early in learning, suggesting that the coding of these variables may be learning dependent.
evidence: This is based on decoding analysis showing poor prediction of reward and licking early in learning.

claim: The coding of reward delivery and licking in dmPFC neurons may be learning dependent.
source: However, activity in these neurons cannot be used to accurately infer reward delivery or licking during sessions early in learning, suggesting that the coding of these variables may be learning dependent.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the differential decoding performance early vs. late in learning.

claim: The timing of CS+ presentation could be decoded based on the activity of all cell clusters, although it was best predicted based on the activity of neurons within Cluster 1.
source: CS+: The timing of CS+ presentation could be decoded based on the activity of all cell clusters, although it was best predicted based on the activity of neurons within Cluster 1.
evidence: This is based on ensemble-specific decoding analysis shown in Figure 3C-D.

claim: The CS- was significantly predicted by Clusters 1, 3, 4, and 5, and was also best predicted based on the activity of Cluster 1.
source: CS-: The CS- was significantly predicted by Clusters 1, 3, 4, and 5, and was also best predicted based on the activity of Cluster 1.
evidence: This is based on ensemble-specific decoding analysis shown in Figure 3C-D.

claim: Activity in Cluster 2, but not other clusters, could be used to significantly discriminate between the CS+ and CS-.
source: CS+ vs. CS-: Activity in Cluster 2, but not other clusters, could be used to significantly discriminate between the CS+ and CS-.
evidence: This is based on ensemble-specific decoding analysis shown in Figure 3C-D.

claim: Activity within Clusters 1, 4, and 5 could be used to detect the reward, with activity in Cluster 4 being the best predictor.
source: Reward: Activity within Clusters 1, 4, and 5 could be used to detect the reward, with activity in Cluster 4 being the best predictor.
evidence: This is based on ensemble-specific decoding analysis shown in Figure 3C-D.

claim: Activity in Cluster 5, but not other clusters, could be used to decode conditioned licking.
source: Licking: Activity in Cluster 5, but not other clusters, could be used to decode conditioned licking.
evidence: This is based on ensemble-specific decoding analysis shown in Figure 3C-D.

claim: Neurons in Cluster 1 show robust responses to CS+, CS-, and reward both early and late in learning.
source: Overall, we found that neurons in Cluster 1, which show excitatory responses to both cues and to the reward late in learning, also show robust responses to the same stimuli early in learning (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on longitudinal tracking data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Neurons in Clusters 2–5 did not show obvious responses before learning during CS+ or CS- trials.
source: In contrast, neurons in Clusters 2–5 did not show obvious responses before learning during CS+ or CS- trials (Figure 4B), suggesting that their activity patterns evolved across conditioning and may therefore be reflective of learning.
evidence: This is based on longitudinal tracking data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The activity patterns of neurons in Clusters 2–5 evolved across conditioning and may be reflective of learning.
source: In contrast, neurons in Clusters 2–5 did not show obvious responses before learning during CS+ or CS- trials (Figure 4B), suggesting that their activity patterns evolved across conditioning and may therefore be reflective of learning.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the longitudinal tracking data.

claim: Neurons in Clusters 2–5 showed CS+ and/or CS- trial response adaptions from early in learning to late in learning behavioral sessions, whereas neurons in Cluster 1 did not.
source: Thus, neurons in Clusters 2–5 showed CS+ and/or CS- trial response adaptions from early in learning to late in learning behavioral sessions, whereas neurons in Cluster 1 did not.
evidence: This is based on statistical comparison of responses across learning shown in Figure 4C-D.

claim: Responses during CS+ and CS- trials late in learning were highly predicted by responses early in learning for all neurons in combination.
source: Interestingly, responses during CS+ and CS- trials late in learning were highly predicted by responses early in learning for all neurons in combination (Figure 4E) and for individual cell clusters except Cluster 2 (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Responses during CS+ and CS- trials late in learning were highly predicted by responses early in learning for individual cell clusters except Cluster 2.
source: Interestingly, responses during CS+ and CS- trials late in learning were highly predicted by responses early in learning for all neurons in combination (Figure 4E) and for individual cell clusters except Cluster 2 (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Although responses in Clusters 2, 4, and 5 adapted from early to late in learning behavioral sessions, responses in these clusters (and Cluster 1) early in learning could be used to predict their subsequent responses late in learning.
source: Thus, although responses in Clusters 2, 4, and 5 adapted from early to late in learning behavioral sessions, responses in these clusters (and Cluster 1) early in learning could be used to predict their subsequent responses late in learning.
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis showing predictive relationships despite adaptation.

claim: Shuffling tracking IDs abolished the correlated response patterns between early and late in learning behavioral sessions.
source: Shuffling abolished the correlated response patterns between early and late in learning behavioral sessions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), confirming that correlated activity patterns from the unshuffled datasets represent similarities in activity across learning for individual neurons – rather than correlated activity patterns within tracked FOVs in general.
evidence: This is based on control analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Correlated activity patterns from the unshuffled datasets represent similarities in activity across learning for individual neurons rather than correlated activity patterns within tracked FOVs in general.
source: Shuffling abolished the correlated response patterns between early and late in learning behavioral sessions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), confirming that correlated activity patterns from the unshuffled datasets represent similarities in activity across learning for individual neurons – rather than correlated activity patterns within tracked FOVs in general.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the shuffling control analysis.

claim: Cross-correlation analysis reveals little lag between neurons in the same cluster, as compared to neurons across clusters, both during early and late in learning behavioral sessions.
source: In further support of this idea, cross-correlation analysis reveals little lag between neurons in the same cluster, as compared to neurons across clusters, both during early and late in learning behavioral sessions (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on cross-correlation analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Mice showed consistent behavioral responses across trials both early in learning and late in learning.
source: Mice showed consistent behavioral responses across trials both early in learning and late in learning (Figure 5A and D; n = 5 mice).
evidence: This is based on trial-by-trial behavioral data shown in Figure 5A and D.

claim: The activity of dmPFC excitatory neurons was consistent across trials during early and late learning behavioral sessions.
source: Furthermore, the activity of dmPFC excitatory neurons (n = 9 FOVs, 416 tracked neurons) was consistent across trials during these behavioral sessions (Figure 5B and E), leading to a strong correlation in activity from trials at the beginning of the session (CS- and CS+ trials 1–10) vs. the end of the session (CS- and CS+ trials 41–50) for all neurons (Figure 5C and F).
evidence: This is based on trial-by-trial neuronal activity data shown in Figure 5B and E.

claim: There was a strong correlation in neuronal activity from trials at the beginning of the session vs. the end of the session for all neurons.
source: Furthermore, the activity of dmPFC excitatory neurons (n = 9 FOVs, 416 tracked neurons) was consistent across trials during these behavioral sessions (Figure 5B and E), leading to a strong correlation in activity from trials at the beginning of the session (CS- and CS+ trials 1–10) vs. the end of the session (CS- and CS+ trials 41–50) for all neurons (Figure 5C and F).
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis shown in Figure 5C and F.

claim: Mice showed equivalent behavioral responses during two late in learning behavioral sessions.
source: Mice showed equivalent behavioral responses during these two late in learning behavioral sessions (Figure 6A), as a repeated t-test revealed no change in cue discrimination scores across days (t3 = 0.217, p-value = 0.835).
evidence: This is based on behavioral data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: A repeated t-test revealed no change in cue discrimination scores across two late learning days (t3 = 0.217, p-value = 0.835).
source: Mice showed equivalent behavioral responses during these two late in learning behavioral sessions (Figure 6A), as a repeated t-test revealed no change in cue discrimination scores across days (t3 = 0.217, p-value = 0.835).
evidence: This is a statistical result from behavioral analysis.

claim: Neuronal responses during both CS+ and CS- trials were highly correlated across two late learning behavioral sessions (CS+: Pearson-R = 0.75, p-value < 0.001; CS-: Pearson-R = 0.30, p-value < 0.001).
source: Furthermore, neuronal responses during both CS+ and CS- trials were highly correlated across these two behavioral sessions (Figure 6B and C; CS+: Pearson-R = 0.75, p-value < 0.001; CS-: Pearson-R = 0.30, p-value < 0.001), unless tracking IDs were shuffled for each FOV (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis shown in Figure 6B-C.

claim: dmPFC excitatory neuronal ensembles display day-to-day response stability after cue-reward learning.
source: Overall, these data suggest that dmPFC excitatory neuronal ensembles display day-to-day response stability after cue-reward learning.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the stability data across two late learning sessions.

claim: Each dmPFC neuronal ensemble may be comprised of a unique set of cell types.
source: Considering the day-to-day stability of dmPFC activity dynamics after learning, our results suggest that each ensemble may be comprised of a unique set of cell types.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed stability of ensemble activity patterns.

claim: Cluster 5 is predicted to be accounted for in part by dmPFC→PVT neurons.
source: Thus, we predict that Cluster 5 is accounted for in part by dmPFC→PVT neurons, although further investigation is required to confirm this idea.
evidence: This is a prediction based on comparison with prior findings about dmPFC→PVT neurons.

claim: It is unlikely that a single projection pathway could be isolated to a single neuronal ensemble.
source: Considering the heterogeneity found even in projection-specific recording studies in dmPFC (Murugan et al., 2017; Otis et al., 2017; Otis et al., 2019; Siciliano et al., 2019; Vander Weele et al., 2018), it is unlikely that a single projection pathway could be isolated to a single neuronal ensemble.
evidence: This is an inference based on prior findings of heterogeneity in projection-specific studies.

claim: Optogenetic inhibition of dmPFC→PVT neurons facilitates cue-reward learning.
source: Interestingly, in that study we found that optogenetic inhibition of dmPFC→PVT neurons facilitates cue-reward learning, whereas optogenetic activation of the pathway prevents learning and cue-evoked reward seeking.
evidence: This is a finding from prior work by the authors.

claim: Optogenetic activation of dmPFC→PVT neurons prevents learning and cue-evoked reward seeking.
source: Interestingly, in that study we found that optogenetic inhibition of dmPFC→PVT neurons facilitates cue-reward learning, whereas optogenetic activation of the pathway prevents learning and cue-evoked reward seeking.
evidence: This is a finding from prior work by the authors.

claim: The immediate early gene NPAS4 is upregulated in reward-responsive, but not aversion-responsive projection neurons in cortex.
source: Although little is known about ensemble-specific gene expression in the dmPFC, cortical excitatory projection neurons are thought to express Camk2α (Dittgen et al., 2004), and there is evidence that the immediate early gene NPAS4 is upregulated in reward-responsive, but not aversion-responsive projection neurons (Ye et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ye et al., 2016.

claim: Cortical excitatory projection neurons are thought to express Camk2α.
source: Although little is known about ensemble-specific gene expression in the dmPFC, cortical excitatory projection neurons are thought to express Camk2α (Dittgen et al., 2004), and there is evidence that the immediate early gene NPAS4 is upregulated in reward-responsive, but not aversion-responsive projection neurons (Ye et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dittgen et al., 2004.

claim: Layer-specific gene expression patterns may be present in dmPFC, such as for genes encoding dopamine receptors, nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, and noradrenergic receptors.
source: Additionally, layer-specific gene expression patterns may be present, such as in the case for genes encoding dopamine receptors (Gaspar et al., 1995), nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (Verhoog et al., 2016), noradrenergic receptors (Santana et al., 2013), and more (for review, see Santana and Artigas, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Previous investigations using in vivo electrophysiology have found coordinated activity among undefined dmPFC cell populations during reward seeking.
source: Previous investigations harnessing in vivo electrophysiology have found coordinated activity among undefined dmPFC cell populations during reward seeking, for example, related to consummatory behavior (licking) in a learning task (Horst and Laubach, 2013), initiation of complex behavioral strategies (Powell and Redish, 2014), recently committed errors in behavioral responding (Powell and Redish, 2014), and behavioral actions based on flexible information (such as rule shifting; Bissonette and Roesch, 2015; Del Arco et al., 2017; Durstewitz et al., 2010; Powell and Redish, 2016; Rodgers and DeWeese, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple prior studies.

claim: One study demonstrated day-to-day stability in behavioral strategy-related firing patterns in dmPFC using waveform matching across days.
source: Using waveform matching across days, one study even demonstrated day-to-day stability in behavioral strategy-related firing patterns (Powell and Redish, 2014), like another study showing stable fos expression, a marker of activated neurons, in dmPFC neurons across days in an appetitive conditioning task (Brebner et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Powell and Redish, 2014.

claim: Another study showed stable fos expression, a marker of activated neurons, in dmPFC neurons across days in an appetitive conditioning task.
source: Using waveform matching across days, one study even demonstrated day-to-day stability in behavioral strategy-related firing patterns (Powell and Redish, 2014), like another study showing stable fos expression, a marker of activated neurons, in dmPFC neurons across days in an appetitive conditioning task (Brebner et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Brebner et al., 2020.

claim: Spectral clustering was chosen based on its improved performance over agglomerative and K-means clustering methods.
source: We chose to use spectral clustering to define unique response dynamics in dmPFC neurons, as opposed to other methods (e.g., agglomerative, K-means), based on preliminary analyses (see Figure 1—figure supplements 3 and 4).
evidence: This is based on comparison of clustering methods shown in Figure 1—figure supplements 3 and 4.

claim: Spectral clustering likely provides better separation of dmPFC neurons into groups due to its ability to separate dynamic and non-singular response features.
source: Although these analyses suggested that spectral clustering provides the best separation of dmPFC neurons into groups, likely due to its ability to separate dynamic and non-singular response features, these methods overall are far from perfect.
evidence: This is an interpretation of why spectral clustering performed better.

claim: Cluster-specific responses or adaptations in activity across learning were generally distinct for CS+ and CS- trials.
source: First, cluster-specific responses or adaptations in activity across learning were generally distinct for CS+ and CS- trials (see Figure 4), suggesting that the observed adaptations are related to cue-reward associative information.
evidence: This is based on data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Cue discrimination, lick, and reward decoding improved over time, despite mice consuming the reward both before and after learning.
source: Second, cue discrimination, lick, and reward decoding improved over time, despite mice consuming the reward both before and after learning (see Figure 5A and D).
evidence: This is based on decoding analysis and behavioral data shown in Figure 5A and D.

claim: Both excitatory and inhibitory responses among subpopulations of dmPFC pyramidal neurons are critical for cue-reward associative learning and cue-driven licking but not licking alone.
source: Finally, previous evidence in the same behavioral task reveals that both excitatory and inhibitory responses among subpopulations of dmPFC pyramidal neurons are critical for cue-reward associative learning and cue-driven licking but not licking alone (Otis et al., 2017; Otis et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Otis et al., 2017 and 2019.

claim: Evidence suggests that identified adaptations in dmPFC activity dynamics are related to cue-reward associative learning.
source: Overall, evidence suggests that our identified adaptations in dmPFC activity dynamics are related to cue-reward associative learning.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of multiple lines of evidence.

claim: The observed conditioned licking responses could be influenced by the effects of water restriction.
source: Another consideration to note is that the observed conditioned licking responses could be influenced by the effects of water restriction, as well as the ratio of sucrose/water used as a reward in our behavioral paradigm (Davey and Cleland, 1982; Harris and Thein, 2005; Tabbara et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a caveat acknowledged by the authors with supporting citations.

claim: Unique aspects of reward seeking may be controlled by distinct neuronal ensembles.
source: Furthermore, our data suggest that unique aspects of reward seeking may be controlled by distinct neuronal ensembles.

claim: Male and female C57BL/6J mice (8 weeks of age/25–35 g at study onset) were used as subjects.
source: Male and female C57BL/6J mice (8 weeks of age/25–35 g at study onset; Jackson Labs) were group-housed pre-operatively and single-housed post-operatively under a reversed 12:12 hr light cycle (lights off at 8:00 a.m.) with access to standard chow and water ad libitum.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental subjects.

claim: Mice were group-housed pre-operatively and single-housed post-operatively.
source: Male and female C57BL/6J mice (8 weeks of age/25–35 g at study onset; Jackson Labs) were group-housed pre-operatively and single-housed post-operatively under a reversed 12:12 hr light cycle (lights off at 8:00 a.m.) with access to standard chow and water ad libitum.
evidence: This is a description of housing conditions.

claim: A virus encoding the calcium indicator GCaMP6s (AAVdj-CaMK2α-GCaMP6s) was unilaterally microinjected into the dmPFC (400 nL; AP, +1.85 mm; ML, −0.50 mm; DV, −2.45 mm).
source: Before lens implantation, a virus encoding the calcium indicator GCaMP6s (AAVdj-CaMK2α-GCaMP6s; UNC Vector Core) was unilaterally microinjected into the dmPFC (specifically targeting prelimbic cortex; 400 nL; anterior-posterior [AP], +1.85 mm; medial-lateral [ML], −0.50 mm; dorsal-ventral [DV], −2.45 mm).
evidence: This is a description of the surgical procedure.

claim: A microendoscopic GRIN lens (4 mm long, 1 mm diameter) was implanted dorsal to dmPFC (AP, +1.85 mm; ML, −0.50 mm; DV, −2.15 mm).
source: Next, a microendoscopic gradient refractive index lens (GRIN lens; 4 mm long, 1 mm diameter; Inscopix) was implanted dorsal to dmPFC (AP, +1.85 mm; ML, −0.50 mm; DV, −2.15 mm) as previously described (Otis et al., 2017; Resendez et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a description of the surgical procedure with citations to prior methods.

claim: Mild water restriction facilitates appetitive learning in head-restrained mice, particularly when the reinforcer is sucrose mixed in water.
source: Mild water restriction facilitates appetitive learning in head-restrained mice, particularly when the reinforcer is sucrose mixed in water (Guo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Guo et al., 2014.

claim: Mild water restriction plus head-restraint results in minimal signs of distress while allowing simultaneous two-photon imaging across many trials of an appetitive behavioral task.
source: Additionally, mild water restriction plus head-restraint results in minimal signs of distress while allowing simultaneous two-photon imaging across many trials of an appetitive behavioral task (Guo et al., 2014; Goltstein et al., 2018; Otis et al., 2017; Otis et al., 2019; Namboodiri et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple prior studies.

claim: Sessions were classified as 'early' or 'late' in learning based on animals' behavioral performance, quantified by their cue discrimination (early, any sessions before auROC < 0.3; late, any sessions after auROC > 0.31).
source: For all behavioral experiments, we classified sessions as 'early' or 'late' in learning based on animals' behavioral performance, quantified by their cue discrimination (early, any sessions before auROC < 0.3; late, any sessions after auROC > 0.31).
evidence: This is a description of the classification criteria used in the study.

claim: Each FOV was separated by at least 50 μm of objective movement in the Z-plane to avoid visualization of the same cells in multiple FOVs.
source: Each FOV was separated by at least 50 μm of objective movement in the Z-plane to avoid visualization of the same cells in multiple FOVs.
evidence: This is a description of the imaging methodology.

claim: Regions of interest around each cell were manually traced using the 'polygon selection' tool in FIJI.
source: Within each FOV, regions of interest around each cell were manually traced using the 'polygon selection' tool in FIJI (Schindelin et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis methodology with citation.

claim: Each region of interest was confirmed independently by an observer who was blind to the experimental conditions.
source: Care was taken to only assign regions of interest to visually distinct cells, and each region of interest was confirmed independently by an observer who was blind to the experimental conditions.
evidence: This is a description of the quality control procedure.
